content: Endometriosis is a medical condition characterized by the presence of functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. The most commonly affected areas include the ovaries, broad ligaments, and surrounding pelvic structures. In some cases, endometriosis can also involve distant sites such as the lungs, ureters, and central nervous system (CNS). The exact cause of endometriosis remains unclear, but several theories have been proposed to explain its pathogenesis. These include Sampson's theory of retrograde menstruation, the coelomic metaplasia theory, and the lymphatic and vascular dissemination theory. These theories attempt to describe how endometrial tissue implants and invades areas outside the uterus. Additionally, immunologic and genetic factors are thought to contribute to the development of the disease. Endometriosis is a significant cause of dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) and dyspareunia (pain during intercourse). It is essential to differentiate endometriosis from other conditions with similar symptoms, such as adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, pelvic congestion syndrome, and submucosal uterine fibroids. The primary goal of medical therapy for endometriosis is to manage pain and reduce the size of endometrial implants. Treatment options include gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists and danazol. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are often used for pain relief. Continuous oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) can be effective for patients with mild to moderate disease. Surgical therapy is reserved for patients with severe disease or those who do not respond to medical treatment. Surgical options include laser ablation or excision of isolated lesions, while total hysterectomy is considered for patients with extensive disease. Historically, endometriosis was first described as adenomyomas in the early 19th century. In the 1920s, it was differentiated from adenomyosis, and detailed descriptions of the disease were provided by Cullen and Sampson. Sampson also proposed the retrograde menstruation theory as a potential explanation for the disease's pathogenesis. Endometriosis is classified into four stages of severity based on the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) scoring system. This classification considers the distribution of lesions and the presence of adhesions. The disease affects approximately 11% of women of reproductive age and is more common among Caucasians than African Americans. It is a leading cause of chronic pelvic pain and infertility. Risk factors for developing endometriosis include early menarche, nulliparity, a positive family history, and congenital cervical stenosis or obstructive lesions in the uterovaginal tract. Standard screening for endometriosis is not recommended. The natural history of the disease varies widely, with presentations ranging from asymptomatic cases to severe symptoms such as premenstrual spotting, cyclic abdominal pain, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and deep endometriosis with dyspareunia, dyschezia (painful defecation), and cyclic rectal bleeding. Complications of endometriosis include infertility, fibrosis, chocolate cysts, and, in rare cases, involvement of other organs such as the lungs. Diagnosis of endometriosis involves a thorough history and physical examination. Patients may report a family history of the disease or congenital abnormalities in the uterovaginal tract. Symptoms include cyclical abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, pain during defecation, and pain during intercourse. On physical examination, findings may include a fixed retroverted uterus, palpable nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments, and narrowing of the posterior fornix. Laboratory findings may reveal iron deficiency anemia and elevated levels of cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) and interleukin-1. Imaging studies such as MRI are more sensitive than CT scans for assessing the anatomical location and severity of the disease. MRI findings typically show hyperintensity on T1-weighted images and hypointensity on T2-weighted images. Ultrasound, particularly transvaginal ultrasound, is useful for differentiating endometriosis from other cystic lesions of the female reproductive system. Endometrial lesions often demonstrate increased vascularity and Doppler flow. Diagnostic laparoscopy remains the gold standard for assessing the severity and extent of the disease. There are no specific electrocardiogram (EKG) findings associated with endometriosis. However, chest X-rays may reveal small bubbles at the level of the right diaphragm and pneumothorax in cases of thoracic endometriosis. CT scans may show catamenial pneumothorax, hemothorax, and lung nodules, but they are not the most sensitive diagnostic tool. Treatment of endometriosis includes both medical and surgical options. Medical therapy focuses on pain management and regression of endometrial lesions. NSAIDs are commonly used for pain relief, while GnRH agonists, danazol, and continuous OCPs are effective in reducing lesion size. Surgical therapy is indicated for patients with advanced disease (stage 3 or 4) or those who fail to respond to medical treatment. Surgical options include laser ablation or excision of isolated lesions, and in severe cases, total hysterectomy may be performed. There are no primary or secondary preventive measures for endometriosis.
